Ya sabes multiplicar dos polinomios: cad: You already know how to multiply two polynomials: every term by every term and then simplify. This topic adds no rule; it points out three products that come up so often that it is worth having them ready in advance. And it turns them round: recognising a product already expanded is factorising, which is the tool Ruffini's rule and equations work with.
Hay tres productos que aparecen tantas v: There are three products that turn up so often that it pays to recognise them at a glance. There is nothing special about them: if you expand them by hand, term by term, they come out on their own. The point is that they appear constantly, and anyone who recognises them saves half a page of working every time.
Y hay algo más importante que desarrolla: And there is something more important than expanding them, which is knowing how to read them backwards. Expanding is easy and mechanical; the hard part, and what the exercises really ask for, is seeing an $x^2+6x+9$ and recognising that it is $(x+3)^2$. That is called factorising and it is half of this topic.

Factorizar es la operación que sostiene: Factorising is the operation that holds up modern cryptography, precisely because with large numbers nobody knows how to do it quickly. Multiplying two 300-digit primes is instant; recovering the factors from the product would take more years than the age of the universe with today's computers. That asymmetry — easy one way, impossible the other — is what protects your bank account.
Los griegos no escribían identidades, la: The Greeks did not write identities, they drew them. Book II of Euclid's Elements, around 300 BC, contains what we now call the special products stated as theorems about areas of rectangles, because for them $a\cdot b$ was a rectangle and $a^2$ was a square. That is why we still say “squared” and “cubed”, and also why the proof with the square cut into four pieces is still the most convincing one.
